newsitem.title: SRI LANKA: S.Lanka sees tea productivity up 50 pct in 10 year.
newsitem.headline: S.Lanka sees tea productivity up 50 pct in 10 year.

text.p: Sri Lankan tea plantations will produce at least 50 percent more tea annually per hectare in 10 years time than they do now, a senior government official said on Monday.

The official, who declined to be identified, said productivity would rise as a result of more efficient use of land, better soil conservation, replanting and improved management practices following privatisation of estates.
He said the average Sri Lankan tea crop per year was now around 1,300 kg per hectare.
"It varies from one region to another, from below 1,000 kg to 3,000 kg," he said. "We expect at least within the next 10 years to reach (an average) level of 2,000 kg."

Sri Lanka has already sold majority stakes and management of 18 of the 23 government-run plantations to private companies and has said the remaining five plantations will be sold off within this year.
The official said Sri Lankan tea output was likely to increase over the next decade even though some areas now under cultivation would be used in future to grow other crops.
The Indian Ocean island produced 258.4 million kg of tea last year, according to the United Nations Food & Agriculture Organisation (FAO).
"Total production is likely to go up by another 25 million kg (over the next 10 years)," the official said. "We see at least two to three percent growth per year."

The official said the gross area of tea cultivation had fallen to between 180,000 and 190,000 hectares from about 240,000 hectares 20 years ago and this process would continue as the new private estates used land more efficiently.
He said most of the tea lands switching to new crops would be in the medium- and high-grown areas, where tea bushes were often older and less productive.

This replanting would gradually shift the majority of tea production to low-grown areas -- plantations closer to sea-level -- which grew tea that was particularly popular in the big markets of Russia and the Middle East.
"Now 50 percent of production is low-grown," he said. "In the medium-term it will grow further. Within the next 10 years it will come to about 60 percent."

The remaining 40 percent would be split between medium and high-grown areas -- from plantations in the hills of central Sri Lanka -- which produce teas traditionally favoured by European and Japanese buyers.
Diversification in some of the higher estates had already led to production of pepper, cloves and nutmeg, he said.
But demand for low-grown varieties was improving.
"Demand is steadily increasing in Russia, in the Middle East...and in developing countries," he said.
